pages.title: The sheath test
pages.for: Is the oversheath sound? The test puts a d.c. voltage across the sheath alone, from the linked screen to an outer electrode.
pages.rule:
V = 4 kV/mm × specified thickness, at most 10 kV d.c.
Hold for 1 minute: no breakdown
Stress = V ÷ thickness
Earthed after: at least 5 minutes (5 × the 1-minute test)

Link conductor, foil and screen at both ends.
Afterwards, take the links off at both ends. Then put the screen earths back on.
Negative to the screen, positive to the outer electrode.
Insulating sheath: earth rod. Semi-conductive sheath: roll spring on its conducting skin.
The cap applies above 2.5 mm.
Other specs use other levels: the client's spec decides.

traps.text: Forgetting the cap: putting 12 kV on a 3.0 mm sheath, when 10 kV is the most.
Using a flat 10 kV, or the factory's 8 kV per mm, on site. The site rule is 4 kV per mm.
traps.cite: Notes p.4; IEC 60229:2007 clause 5 and routine test (research)

traps.text: Leaving a metal layer unlinked. Join conductor, foil and screen at both ends.
Putting the positive on the wrong outer electrode for the sheath type.
Leaving the screen earths off after the test.
traps.cite: Nexans, TR-XLPE long-life cables; Dmitriev, Semiconductive layer over the cable sheath (research)

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: A core's oversheath is 2.0 mm thick. What d.c. voltage does the sheath test put across it, and for how long?
pages.alt: V = 4 kV per mm × thickness = 4 × 2.0 = 8.0 kV. That is under the 10 kV cap, so 8.0 kV d.c., held for 1 minute. 4.0 kV leaves out the thickness. 10.0 kV is the cap, which only applies above 2.5 mm.
pages.html:
V = 4 kV per mm × thickness = 4 × 2.0 = 8.0 kV. That is under the 10 kV cap, so 8.0 kV d.c., held for 1 minute.

4.0 kV leaves out the thickness. 10.0 kV is the cap, which only applies above 2.5 mm.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: Each core's oversheath is the plastic layer outside its screen and foil. Its job is to keep water away from the insulation. The sheath test checks it on its own. It puts a d.c. voltage across the sheath, from the screen inside to a conductor on its outer face. It runs after the IR test and before VLF. It looks for damage done while the cable was laid.
pages.alt: XLPE break in the sheath oversheath water trees: screen and foil months or years later water If it is skipped A hole in the sheath does not fail the cable on day one. It lets water in. Under the working voltage, that water can slowly grow water trees in the XLPE until the insulation fails. Sheath faults can cost the whole cable.
pages.html:
If it is skipped

A hole in the sheath does not fail the cable on day one. It lets water in. Under the working voltage, that water can slowly grow water trees in the XLPE until the insulation fails. Sheath faults can cost the whole cable.

pages.name: The why: volts per millimetre
pages.text: The sheath test is an insulation test on the sheath alone. The screen inside is one electrode. A conductor on the sheath's outer face is the other, the outer electrode. If the sheath has a hole, it breaks down there. Current flows through the hole and the test set trips. Plastic breaks down when the field across it gets too strong. That field is the voltage per millimetre of thickness. Put the same voltage across a thin sheath and a thick one. The thin one takes far more stress. So the rule scales the voltage with the thickness. It sets 4 kV d.c. per millimetre, at most 10 kV, for 1 minute. Use the thickness specified on the data sheet. Every sheath up to 2.5 mm gets the same 4 kV per mm. Above 2.5 mm the rule caps the voltage at 10 kV. A thicker sheath is simply tested more gently. Up to 2.5 mm the voltage rises 4 kV for every millimetre, and the stress stays at 4.00 kV/mm. String B's 2.2 mm sheath takes 8.8 kV. From 2.5 mm the voltage stays at the 10 kV cap. So the stress falls, down to 2.50 kV/mm at 4.0 mm. In the factory, the d.c. test on a new sheath uses 8 kV per mm. The site test is half that. Not every spec uses the per-millimetre rule. Some specs use a flat 10 kV d.c. for 1 minute instead. The client's test spec sets the level on the job.

4 × 4.0 would be 16.0 kV, over the cap. So the test holds at 10.0 kV, and the stress falls to 10.0 ÷ 4.0 = 2.50 kV/mm.

In the factory, the d.c. test on a new sheath uses 8 kV per mm. The site test is half that. Not every spec uses the per-millimetre rule. Some specs use a flat 10 kV d.c. for 1 minute instead. The client's test spec sets the level on the job.

pages.name: What to link, and where the leads go
pages.text: The test must stress the sheath and nothing else. So the conductor, the foil and the screen are linked together at both ends. The foil sits right under the sheath. Once linked, it carries the full test voltage onto the sheath's inner face. The conductor is at the same voltage, so the XLPE between conductor and screen has nothing across it. The negative lead goes to the linked screen. The positive lead goes to the outer electrode. That is the same way round as the IR test: positive on the outside. The outer electrode must reach the whole length of the sheath, so the whole sheath is tested. Which one you use depends on the sheath. On an insulating sheath the positive goes to an earth rod. On a semi-conductive sheath it goes through a roll spring to the sheath's conducting skin. Either way the negative is on the linked screen. The sheath takes the 8.8 kV and the XLPE takes none. Leave the conductor earthed instead of linked, and the XLPE takes the 8.8 kV too. Assume String B's core sheaths are semi-conductive. On a job, read the sheath type off the data sheet. Each core's own sheath is the one tested. The armour and outer yarn sit outside all three cores and are not tested.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: Cable P has a 1.5 mm sheath and cable Q a 3.5 mm sheath. Each is tested at its own correct voltage. Which sheath takes the higher stress per millimetre?
pages.alt: P takes 4 × 1.5 = 6.0 kV. That gives 6.0 ÷ 1.5 = 4.00 kV/mm. Q works out at 4 × 3.5 = 14.0 kV. That is over the cap, so it gets 10.0 kV. That gives 10.0 ÷ 3.5 = 2.86 kV/mm. The cap leaves a thick sheath less stressed.
options: Both the same, 4 kV per mm

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: A cable with insulating core sheaths, 1.8 mm thick by its data sheet. A practice value. On a 1.8 mm insulating sheath, first earth both ends. Link foil, screen and conductor at both ends. Put the negative on the screen and the positive on the earth rod. Then lift the earths under control. Hold 4 × 1.8 = 7.2 kV d.c. for 1 minute. It passes with no breakdown. Then discharge in the usual order. Keep the screen and the core earthed for at least 5 minutes. Take the links off at both ends, then put the screen earths back before the cable is energised.
pages.alt: 1 Earth the screen and the conductor at both ends. 2 Link foil, screen and conductor together at both ends. 3 Negative lead to the linked screen. Positive lead to the earth rod. 4 Tell the far end. Lift the earths under control, with access restricted at both ends. 5 V = 4 × 1.8 = 7.2 kV d.c., under the 10 kV cap. Hold it for 1 minute. 6 It passes if the sheath holds 7.2 kV for the full minute with no breakdown. 7 Discharge it as after the IR test. Wait for the display to show discharged. Then use the discharge stick, then the hook stick, then the hand earth.
pages.html:
1

Earth the screen and the conductor at both ends.

2

Link foil, screen and conductor together at both ends.

3

Negative lead to the linked screen. Positive lead to the earth rod.

4

Tell the far end. Lift the earths under control, with access restricted at both ends.

5

V = 4 × 1.8 = 7.2 kV d.c., under the 10 kV cap. Hold it for 1 minute.

6

It passes if the sheath holds 7.2 kV for the full minute with no breakdown.

7

Discharge it as after the IR test. Wait for the display to show discharged. Then use the discharge stick, then the hook stick, then the hand earth. Earth the screen and the core at both ends. Keep them earthed for at least 5 × the 1 minute the voltage was on, so at least 5 minutes.

Line 7 matters as much as the test. The sheath holds charge, just as the core does. Before the cable is energised, take the links off at both ends. Then put the screen earths back on at both ends. Screens have been left unearthed after sheath tests, then energised that way for days.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain why a failed sheath test matters even when the main insulation passes.
pages.why: A model answer: The sheath is there to keep water away from the insulation. If it is holed, water gets in. Under the electric field, that water grows water trees in the XLPE. They grow slowly, over months or years. So the cable does not fail on day one. The main insulation can pass every test today and still fail later. Sheath faults are common. Cables fail more often from sheath problems than from the main insulation. A sheath fault left in place can cost the whole cable.
